Compare two research ideas for the SAME research problem and pick the stronger one.

Research problem: Can MVFA's segmentation adapters learn transferable localisation from image-level labels alone? Today they learn only from pixel masks of BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC. We replace the Dice and Focal seg_loss with a multiple-instance objective applied at all four levels to the segmentation-branch patch-to-text similarity map (mean of the top 2% patch anomaly probabilities; max and mean pooling as ablations), and train on all five source datasets with masks discarded. Primary question and hypothesis: because every patch is scored against a shared text anchor, image-level supervision aligns patch-level evidence with the text 'abnormal' direction, so the learned localisation transfers to the unseen modality and retains at least 80% of mask-supervised MVFA's pixel-level AUROC (with PRO and image AUROC also reported). A visual-only MIL control (same operator on a linear patch classifier without text anchors) tests whether text anchoring is responsible. Secondary analyses: per-level localisation quality, and a label-budget comparison on two held-out modalities between image-labelled training and mask-supervised training on 10%, 30% and 100% of the masked images.

A stronger idea is one whose proposed change acts on the SPECIFIC mechanism of the target method that causes the problem (here: the released MVFA code and its verified behaviour), rather than a generic improvement that would apply to any anomaly detector.

Judge on:
1. Specificity. Would this idea plausibly solve THIS problem in THIS method better than a generic alternative? A mechanism that applies equally to any model and any problem is WEAKER, not stronger, because it does not explain why it fixes this problem.
2. Evidence. Is the proposed mechanism supported by the cited literature or by verified properties of the code and the benchmark?
3. Testability. Does the idea make a concrete, falsifiable prediction that can be checked on BMAD with one Colab GPU?

Explicitly DO NOT reward: length or polish of the write-up, stacking many modules, vague "add an attention/adapter module" proposals, or ideas that need data, labels or compute that are not available.

Idea A:
TITLE: Patch-level positive-unlabelled learning: normal-image patches as labelled negatives, abnormal-image patches as unlabelled
SUMMARY: Recast mask-free training of MVFA's segmentation adapters as positive-unlabelled (PU) learning at the patch level, using the non-negative PU risk estimator with a per-dataset class prior (expected lesion fraction) estimated from image-labelled data.
HYPOTHESIS: Non-negative PU learning with an estimated patch-level class prior retains at least 85% of mask-supervised MVFA's held-out pixel-AUROC margin over chance and outperforms asymmetric top-k MIL by at least 1.5 pixel-AUROC points, because it uses every patch of abnormal images rather than only the top-k.
RATIONALE: The parent's key insight — every patch of a normal image is normal — is exactly the labelled side of a PU problem: here the known class is 'normal' (labelled negatives) and abnormal images contribute an unlabelled mixture of normal and abnormal patches. PU learning theory gives an unbiased risk estimator for this setting once the mixture proportion (the fraction of anomalous patches in abnormal images) is known; MIL's top-k is a heuristic stand-in for that proportion. The proportion can be estimated without masks by mixture proportion estimation between normal-image and abnormal-image patch score distributions.
METHOD: 1) Patch classifier = MVFA's segmentation-branch patch-text logit z = t(cos(f, T_abn) - cos(f, T_nor)) + b. 2) Class prior pi_d for each source dataset d: mixture proportion estimation (best-bin estimator) on the zero-shot patch scores of normal vs abnormal images. 3) nnPU loss: with N = normal-image patches (labelled 'normal') and U = abnormal-image patches with mixing weight pi, R = (1 - pi) E_N[l(z, normal)]... implemented with the standard nnPU estimator (Kiryo et al.) where the negative class is labelled, max(0, ...) correction on the unlabelled term. 4) Sigmoid loss, lr 1e-4, 50 epochs; balanced batches of 4 normal + 4 abnormal images from the same dataset. 5) Code: loss.py nnpu_loss(); estimate_prior.py; train_zero.py.
EXPERIMENT: BMAD zero-shot leave-one-modality-out (RESC and OCT17 held out together); no source masks used by the proposed variants; checkpoints selected on source-modality validation splits by image AUROC; mask-supervised MVFA re-run under the same rule as reference; 3 seeds; pixel metrics on held-out BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC. Baselines: asymmetric SigLIP-MIL; top-k MIL; mask-supervised MVFA. Ablations: prior misspecification (x0.5, x2); estimated vs oracle prior (from masks, analysis only). Metrics: held-out pixel AUROC, PRO, image AUROC; prior estimation error (analysis). Falsification: no gain over asymmetric MIL.

Idea B:
TITLE: Bank-gated asymmetric MIL: positives must be both text-abnormal and unlike any normal patch of the dataset
SUMMARY: In asymmetric SigLIP-MIL, choose the positive patches of an abnormal image only among those that the dataset's normal-patch bank also flags as unusual, and use the bank distance as a soft target weight, combining text-based and memory-based evidence from image labels.
HYPOTHESIS: Gating MIL positives with normal-bank distance increases held-out PRO by at least 2 points over asymmetric MIL alone and over normal-bank pseudo-masks alone, while retaining at least 85% of mask-supervised MVFA's pixel-AUROC margin over chance.
RATIONALE: The reviews ranked these two parents highest but noted complementary failure modes: MIL can select salient normal structures that align with the abnormal text anchor, and bank distances can flag normal anatomical variability. A patch flagged by both is far more likely to be a lesion. The combination keeps a single loss and uses the bank only for selection and weighting, so its cost is close to that of either parent.
METHOD: 1) Build per-dataset normal coreset banks (10%) of frozen level-3 tokens from image-labelled normal training images; bank distance d_j = 1 - max cosine. 2) For each abnormal image, candidate set = patches with d_j above the dataset's normal 95th percentile; MIL positives = top-k (k = 6) by segmentation probability within the candidate set (fall back to global top-k if fewer than k candidates). 3) Positive term weighted by w_j = d_j / max d. 4) Normal images: all-patches-normal SigLIP term. 5) Code: make_banks.py; loss.py gated_asym_mil(); train_zero.py; lr 1e-4, 50 epochs.
EXPERIMENT: BMAD zero-shot leave-one-modality-out (RESC and OCT17 held out together); no source masks used by the proposed variants; checkpoints selected on source-modality validation splits by image AUROC; mask-supervised MVFA re-run under the same rule as reference; 3 seeds; pixel metrics on held-out BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC. Baselines: asymmetric MIL; normal-bank pseudo-masks; mask-supervised MVFA. Ablations: gating percentile; with/without soft weights; bank level. Metrics: held-out pixel AUROC, PRO, image AUROC; precision of selected positives (analysis). Falsification: no PRO gain over both parents.

Respond in exactly this format:
REASONING: <one to three sentences explaining your choice>
CONFIDENCE: <HIGH | MEDIUM | LOW>
WINNER=<A | B | TIE>
